chaos

/KAY-oss/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Chaos means absolute disorder and confusion.

During the Saturday dinner rush, one broken oven plunged the restaurant kitchen into chaos — servers colliding, tickets piling up, and three dishes burning at once.

Example

When the fire alarm blared through the crowded office tower, the lobby collapsed into chaos as hundreds of workers pushed toward the exits at once.

All order broke down at the same moment — no lines, no calm, no system, just hundreds of people moving in confusion. That total collapse of order is chaos.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

mayhem: Mayhem is disorder with violence in it — brawls, smashed windows, real damage being done. Chaos is about order itself collapsing, violent or not: a kitchen in chaos may just be tickets piling up and dishes burning. Mayhem needs harm; chaos only needs the total loss of order.

disorder: Disorder is the neutral, all-purpose word for the absence of arrangement or control, and it comes in every size, from an untidy drawer upward. Chaos sits at the far extreme: order has completely broken down. Mild disorder is normal life; chaos is the moment nothing works at all.

turmoil: Turmoil is agitated churning — minds, crowds, and whole countries are in turmoil when they seethe with confusion and unrest. Chaos describes outward order collapsing: no lines, no system, nothing where it belongs. A person can sit still in inner turmoil, while chaos always shows in the scene around you.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

order: a state where everything is arranged and controlled

calm: peaceful stillness, free of disturbance

Where it sits · how completely order has broken down

disarray → chaos → pandemonium

disarray vs. chaos: A room in disarray is merely untidy; a room in chaos has lost every trace of order.

pandemonium vs. chaos: Chaos is complete disorder; pandemonium piles deafening noise and wild uproar on top of it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — chaos: borrowed whole from Greek khaos, "a vast, gaping void" — the formless emptiness the Greeks imagined before the world began

Put it together: Chaos doesn't break into smaller word-parts — it came into English whole from Greek khaos, the yawning void before creation. Total disorder is like tumbling back into that formless void.

Use the root in a new word: chaotic: The chaotic scramble for seats ended the moment the usher began directing people row by row.

Word Building

Word Choice

Neutral — everyday & news

Chaos is an extreme word: it means order has completely broken down, not that things are a little messy. Common collocations: descend into chaos, utter chaos, complete chaos. For milder messes, English prefers gentler relatives like disarray or disorder.
